howItWorks.intro: Behind the single number, the calculator weighs the same two dimensions that social-connection researchers study separately: how much contact you have (close relationships and weekly meaningful interactions) and how connected you feel (sense of belonging and loneliness frequency). Combining both avoids the common trap of measuring only one side of the equation — a busy calendar doesn't guarantee belonging, and a quiet one doesn't guarantee loneliness.

rules.name: Social Score
rules.formula: Score = Relationships + Interactions + Belonging + Loneliness factors

howItWorks.outro: The result is a self-reflection snapshot, not a clinical screening instrument — it can't replace an assessment from a therapist or physician, and it isn't trying to. If your score is lower than you expected, the more useful question is usually why: is it recent (a move, a breakup, a demanding season at work) or persistent? A temporary dip after a life change is common and often resolves as routines rebuild; persistent, distressing disconnection is worth raising with a professional.

faq.question: What's the difference between loneliness and social isolation?
faq.answer: Isolation is objective — how many people you actually see or talk to, and how often. Loneliness is subjective — the gap between the connection you have and the connection you want. You can be isolated without feeling lonely (plenty of people are genuinely content with solitude), and you can feel lonely without being isolated (a crowded room or a busy group chat doesn't guarantee a sense of belonging). This calculator asks about both because either measure alone tells an incomplete story.

faq.question: Why does the calculator ask about close relationships and weekly interactions separately?
faq.answer: Because they capture different things. Someone with 3 close relationships they speak to roughly weekly, plus 2 casual friendships seen about once a month, is getting steady, dependable contact even though their headcount is modest. Someone with 15 acquaintances but no one they talk to on a weekly basis may have a wider network on paper yet less real support day to day. Frequency and closeness tend to matter more than raw headcount in the underlying research, so the calculator tracks them as separate inputs rather than folding everything into one contact-list number.

faq.question: Is a low score something to worry about?
faq.answer: Not automatically. A dip after a move, a breakup, or a demanding stretch at work is common and usually temporary as routines rebuild. What's worth paying attention to is a pattern — a consistently low score over several weeks or months, especially alongside loneliness marked "Often" or "Always" — rather than a single rough result on a single day.

faq.question: Can this calculator diagnose loneliness or a mental health condition?
faq.answer: No. It's a self-reflection tool, not a clinical or diagnostic instrument, and it isn't a substitute for a validated screening scale or an evaluation by a professional. If persistent loneliness or isolation is affecting your wellbeing, sleep, or daily functioning, that's worth discussing with a doctor or counselor.

faq.question: How can I improve my score without overhauling my life?
faq.answer: Start with frequency, not novelty: a recurring low-effort touchpoint — a standing weekly call, a regular class — tends to do more for connection over time than an occasional big event. Prioritize quality time (real conversation) over parallel time (scrolling or watching side by side), and consider joining one recurring group where you'll see the same people repeatedly, since repetition is what turns acquaintances into close relationships.

faq.question: Why does the research compare chronic loneliness to smoking?
faq.answer: The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory on the epidemic of loneliness in America found that chronic social disconnection carries health risks comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day, including higher risk of heart disease, stroke, and premature death. That comparison is meant to convey scale, not to suggest an occasional lonely evening carries the same risk — it's the chronic, persistent pattern the research links to those outcomes, not a bad week.

faq.question: Is the Social Connection Score Calculator free to use?
faq.answer: Yes. It runs entirely in your browser, requires no signup, and you can retake it as often as you like — every few months, for example, to see whether your score is trending the direction you want.

howWeCalculate.intro: Enter your four inputs and the calculator works through them the same way every time — no hidden weighting changes between visits, so you can retake it later and compare honestly.
steps: Enter the number of close relationships you currently have — people you'd call in a genuine crisis, not your full contact list.
Enter your typical weekly meaningful interactions — conversations with real back-and-forth, not brief transactional exchanges like ordering coffee.
Rate your sense of belonging from 1 to 10, then select how often you feel lonely, from Rarely to Always, based on the last few weeks rather than just today.
The calculator combines the four inputs into a Social Health Score and a plain-language assessment, calculated instantly in your browser — nothing you enter is sent anywhere.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: This score is a self-reflection estimate based on general social-connection research, not a validated clinical scale (such as the UCLA Loneliness Scale), and it isn't a diagnosis of anything. If persistent loneliness or isolation is affecting your daily life, sleep, or mood, talk with a doctor or counselor — they can help in ways a calculator can't.

whenToUse.intro: This calculator is most useful as a periodic check-in rather than a one-time verdict — think of it the way you'd think of a step count: informative in the moment, more informative as a trend over weeks and months.
scenarios: After a major life change — a move, a new job, a breakup, retirement, or becoming a parent — when your usual social routines have been disrupted
When you want an honest baseline before deliberately investing more time in relationships, so you can measure whether the effort is actually working

If you've noticed more time spent on parallel activities, like scrolling beside a partner or roommate, than on actual conversation, and want a nudge to check whether that's showing up in how connected you feel
When comparing how you feel now to a few months ago, by retaking the calculator and comparing results over time
As a starting point for a conversation with a therapist, coach, or doctor about your social health — not as a replacement for that conversation

sections.title: What the Social Connection Score Measures
sections.body: The Social Connection Score Calculator turns four everyday inputs — how many close relationships you have, how many meaningful interactions you have in a typical week, how strong your sense of belonging feels on a 1–10 scale, and how often you feel lonely — into a single snapshot of your current social health. It exists because loneliness and social isolation get lumped together constantly, even though they're different things. Isolation is objective: how many people you actually see or talk to, and how often. Loneliness is subjective: the gap between the connection you have and the connection you want. You can live alone, see few people in a week, and feel entirely content — that's solitude, not loneliness. You can also be surrounded by coworkers, family, or a busy group chat and still feel disconnected — that's loneliness without isolation. This calculator asks about both axes on purpose: a score built only on contact frequency would miss the person with ten weekly interactions who still feels invisible, and a score built only on feelings would miss the person whose isolation is real but hasn't registered emotionally yet.

sections.title: Why Connection Quality Outweighs Contact Quantity
sections.body: The research behind social-connection scoring consistently points the same direction: a small number of close, reciprocal relationships tends to predict wellbeing better than a large network of casual contacts. Consider two people. The first has 3 close relationships they speak with roughly weekly, plus 2 casual friendships seen about once a month — call that 3 close ties and around 7–8 meaningful interactions in an average week once the weekly check-ins are counted. The second person has 15 acquaintances — old classmates, neighbors, people from a hobby group — but no one they talk to on a close, weekly basis; their meaningful interactions in a typical week might be 1 or 2, and mostly small talk. Even though the second person's address book is five times larger, the first will typically score meaningfully higher on a connection-health measure, because frequency and closeness of contact — not raw headcount — are what social-support research ties to lower stress, better sleep, and reduced cardiovascular risk. That's also why belonging and loneliness frequency sit alongside the two headcount-style inputs here: two people with identical relationship counts can land in very different places depending on how connected they actually feel.

sections.title: How to Use This Score, and Its Limits
sections.body: Treat the result as a starting point for reflection, not a diagnosis. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory on the epidemic of loneliness described chronic social disconnection as carrying health risks comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day — a striking figure, and one reason the topic deserves to be taken seriously rather than dismissed as a soft concern. At the same time, one low score on one day doesn't mean something is wrong, and this tool can't account for your individual circumstances, temperament, or life stage — plenty of people are genuinely content with a smaller circle and infrequent contact. If your score is consistently low, or if loneliness shows up as "Often" or "Always" over weeks rather than a single rough patch, and it's affecting your mood, sleep, or motivation, that's worth raising with a doctor, therapist, or counselor rather than something to work out alone with a number on a screen.

howToSteps.title: Count Your Close Relationships
howToSteps.description: Enter the number of people you'd genuinely turn to in a hard moment — not your whole social circle, just the ones who'd actually pick up the phone.

howToSteps.title: Estimate Weekly Meaningful Interactions
howToSteps.description: Think through a typical week and count real conversations, not brief hellos — a call with a parent counts; a nod to a neighbor usually doesn't.

howToSteps.title: Rate Belonging and Loneliness Frequency
howToSteps.description: Score your sense of belonging from 1 to 10, then choose how often you've felt lonely lately, from Rarely to Always — answer for the last few weeks, not just today.

howToSteps.title: Calculate and Read Your Assessment
howToSteps.description: Select Calculate to see your Social Health Score and its plain-language assessment, then use it to decide whether anything in your routine is worth changing.

tips: Weight quality over headcount when answering — three relationships where you can be fully yourself matter more to what this score is measuring than fifteen names you rarely speak to.

Low-effort, regular contact (a weekly call, a standing coffee, a recurring group class) tends to sustain connection better than infrequent big gatherings — if your weekly-interactions number is low, that's often the easiest input to move.

Joining something recurring — a league, a class, a volunteer shift, a community or faith group — builds relationships faster than one-off events, because it guarantees repeated contact with the same people over time.
Notice the difference between quality time and parallel time: watching a show side by side isn't the same as a conversation, and only the latter tends to move your sense-of-belonging rating.
If your loneliness frequency is "Often" or "Always" and has been for weeks, treat that as more informative than the overall score — it's the input most worth acting on first.
